summary: Proposes a device-independent description of a graphical display, so graphics sent over the ARPANET can be turned into a picture on whatever device the receiving user has. It updates RFC 125 and mentions the form machine idea in RFC 94.

eli5.summary: If you describe a drawing in plain words, anyone can draw it on their own paper. This proposal is a language for describing pictures that any screen can follow.

questions: what is a device independent graphical display description
how can graphics be sent across the network
subtitle: A proposed way to describe pictures so any graphics display on the ARPANET can draw them.

tldr.problem: Graphical display processors on the network vary widely, so graphical information sent between hosts needs a form that does not depend on one device.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a network standard graphics description stream of byte-coded commands that define named display lists, image areas and drawing items, which the using host converts for its own device.
tldr.outcome: It is a proposal that updates RFC 125, and it leaves interaction with the picture largely open. The unit metadata lists RFC 181 as an update to it.

today: This RFC updates RFC 125, and the unit metadata lists RFC 181 as an update to it. Its status is given as unknown.

sections.title: A Device Independent Description
sections.content:
The RFC describes a device-independent description of a display to ease sending graphics over the network. The using host makes whatever conversions are needed to realize the picture on a specific device. It is also possible to interpose a form machine as proposed in RFC 94. Some of the entities were first discussed in RFC 86.

The target is a refresh display with point, vector and character drawing, such as the IBM 2250, IMLAC PDS-1, DEC 338 and DEC 340, and the Evans and Sutherland LDS-1. Storage tube devices such as the ARDS and Tektronix can serve as clumsy interactive devices, and hard copy devices like plotters can be used at the using host's discretion.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing a finished picture that only fits one kind of paper, you mail instructions for drawing it, and each person draws it with their own pens.

sections.title: Streams, Lists and the Screen
sections.content:
The network standard graphics description stream (NGDS) holds the descriptions, data and operators needed to produce a display. An interpreter parses it into commands, which define named display lists (NGDL). A list interpreter (NGLI) executes the lists and controls the beam, using a list pointer (NGLP) and an execution stack (NGES) so it can work recursively.

The standard screen is rectangular. Positions are (x,y) pairs of 16-bit unsigned fractions measured from the left and bottom edges, so coordinates run from 0.0 up to just under 1. No resolution is specified. The screen can be split into image areas, each with a 16-bit name and lower-left and upper-right corners; the main area, name 0, covers the whole screen. Characters are assumed to be .014 screen width by .025 screen height, giving 72 characters and 40 lines.
sections.eli5: The screen is a sheet of paper where every spot is described as a fraction across and up, so a big screen and a small one can both follow the same directions.

sections.title: Commands and List Items
sections.content:
Commands are an eight-bit code followed by parameters. ERASE (0) clears the screen, DEFINE LIST (1) defines or redefines a named list, DEFINE IMAGE AREA (2) defines an area, and TRANSLATE LIST (3), SCALE LIST (4) and ROTATE LIST (5) change all instances of a list without resending it.

A list holds items, also in prefix format and ending with an end-list item. Items open, reset or clear an image area, move the beam, display the current point, draw a vector, or display characters. EXECUTE LIST acts like a subroutine call and COPY LIST like a macro. Two mode items set brightness, blinking, color and, for vectors, texture, or for characters, size and orientation. Devices that cannot support a mode treat it as a no-op.
sections.eli5: The picture is a recipe: erase the board, then a list of steps such as move the pen, draw a line, write some letters, or follow another recipe first.

sections.title: Interaction With the Picture
sections.content:
The RFC says that interacting with the displayed picture has yet to be properly addressed. Key boards and function keys can be handled as standard messages from the graphics device to the serving host. Pointing at the picture is harder, because only the serving host can probably tie a selected point to a meaningful entity such as a list.

It separates synchronous devices, such as light pens, which cause attention while a given item is being executed, from asynchronous devices, which can interact at any time. A synchronous INTERACTION report carries the current image area, list name, origin, list pointer and the execution stack entries. An asynchronous one carries the image area name, the coordinates within it and the screen coordinates.
sections.eli5: Drawing is easy; touching a drawing and knowing which part you touched is harder, so the note only sketches how to report where you pointed.

items.label: OPEN IMAGE AREA
items.desc: Following items are adjusted to fit the named area.

items.label: RESET IMAGE AREA
items.desc: Move the beam to the lower left corner of the area.

items.label: CLEAR IMAGE AREA
items.desc: Erase the area, then reset it.

items.label: MOVE BEAM
items.desc: Move to (x,y) relative to the current origin.

items.label: DISPLAY VECTOR
items.desc: Draw from the current point to (x,y).

items.label: DISPLAY CHARACTERS
items.desc: Display n characters from the current point.

items.label: EXECUTE LIST
items.desc: Run a named list, like a subroutine call.

items.label: COPY LIST
items.desc: Copy a named list in place, like a macro.

items.label: EXECUTE TABLE
items.desc: Run a list of coordinate pairs in point or vector mode.

items.label: END LIST
items.desc: Marks the end of a list.

items.label: TABLE
items.desc: States that the list has n (x,y) pairs.

items.label: Set character mode
items.desc: Brightness, blink, color, size and orientation.
